question: How did Sachin Monga describe Substack’s process for developing its writer-recommendation feature, from spotting reader behavior to deciding what to build?
expected_points: The team noticed readers were discovering other Substacks through writer-centered paths, such as guest posts and commenters’ profiles.
They considered algorithmic recommendations but worried that would reduce writers’ control over the reader experience.
They chose a simple approach: let writers opt in and recommend others in the subscription flow, then tried it despite skepticism about whether it would work.

sections.heading: Start with behavior already emerging
sections.content: Readers were discovering other Substacks through the writer they already followed. Examples included guest posts and, when comments were enabled, clicking a commenter’s profile to see other Substacks they read. Monga saw potential in scaling this cross-pollination as the platform gained more writers and readers.

sections.heading: Compare the obvious solution against Substack’s principles
sections.content: One option was to recommend newsletters directly to readers based on their reading habits, similar in form to Facebook’s People You May Know. But inserting recommendations into a post or email could show readers unrelated content in a space controlled by a writer, weakening writer control. Substack’s principle was to favor approaches that preserve writer and reader agency.

sections.heading: Choose writer-led recommendations and test them
sections.content: The simpler, more writer-controlled alternative was to ask writers whom they recommended and place those recommendations in the subscribe flow. Monga said Chris was skeptical because success depended on several things: writers opting in, selecting good recommendations, and giving those recommendations enough visibility. As part of the rollout, the team treated the feature as optional, called 10 writers who might be interested, mocked it up, and gathered feedback rather than switching it on for everyone at once. The feature nevertheless took off quickly; recommendations also prompted emails telling recommended writers who was sending readers their way, creating a goodwill-driven viral loop.

answer.summary: Monga said Substack started from organic, writer-led discovery, considered algorithmic recommendations, then chose a simple, curated option that kept writers in control: ask them whom they recommend and show those picks during sign-up. The team tested the idea with writers before rolling it out. [S1, S2, S3, S4, S6, S7]

sections.heading: Start with behavior already happening
sections.content: Readers were discovering other Substacks through the writer they already followed. Examples included guest posts, and clicking a commenter’s profile to see other Substacks that person read. Monga saw potential in amplifying this cross-pollination as the platform’s supply of writers and readers grew. [S1, S2]

sections.heading: Compare options against the control principle
sections.content: A straightforward alternative was to recommend newsletters based on readers’ habits, like a general recommendation unit in a post or email. But Monga worried that could take control away from the writer and show readers content unrelated to the writer they chose. So the team went back to the simplest approach that put writers in control: ask writers whom they recommend and place those recommendations in the subscribe flow. [S3, S4, S5]

sections.heading: Try the harder, curated approach and learn with writers
sections.content: The idea required writers to opt in, choose good recommendations, and have those picks surfaced broadly enough to matter. Chris was skeptical that all those steps would come together. Monga said they tried it and it took off quickly; recommendations also created a goodwill loop, as recommended writers received an email saying who recommended them and how many readers were being sent their way. For development, the team mocked up the idea, sought feedback from writers, and ran a small pilot rather than launching it to everyone immediately. [S4, S6, S7]
